lesson.subtitle: Lesson 22 — Talking About Past Experiences
lesson.title_tag: Professor View — Vanessa Giuriati | Lesson 22 — Talking About Past Experiences
lesson.grammar_point: present perfect vs simple past for experiences (Have you ever...? / I went in April)

listenings.text: My favorite question at a dinner table is this one: have you ever done something you were sure you would never do? It works every time, because everybody has one story like that. I asked it last month, and a very quiet man at the end of the table told us he had once sold his car to pay for a month in Portugal. He was thirty-one. He had never traveled alone before, and he did not speak a word of the language. He said the first week was ordinary and a little lonely. Then he got the chance to work in a small bakery, and everything changed. That month is still the highlight of his life, and he talks about it as a once in a lifetime thing. What I love is that on paper it was a terrible decision. He came home with no car and no money. But ever since that trip, he says, he has never been afraid of starting over.

Here is a small thing that changes how people hear your stories. When you say I have been to Rome, you are talking about your life so far: the experience is in your bag, and nobody asks when. When you say I went to Rome in 2019, you have put it on a date, and now the story has a place and a time. Native speakers move between the two without thinking. They open with the experience, have you ever been to Rome, I have, and then they zoom in, I went two summers ago and it rained for six days. Notice the order. General first, specific second. If you start with the date, the listener has nothing to hold on to. So next time somebody asks about your travels, do not begin with a year. Begin with what you have done. The details are the second sentence, and they only land after the first one does.

extra_audio.text: First, I open with the experience itself: I have been to Japan, and I have never regretted it. Then I zoom in with a date in the simple past: I went last April and stayed for five days. After that, I give one small detail that makes it real, like the empty temple at six in the morning. Next, I say how I felt, including the uncomfortable part, like the day I was homesick. In the end, I say what changed: ever since that trip, my bucket list keeps getting longer.

reading.rtitle: Solo, Finally — a post from a personal blog
paras: I have traveled a lot for work, but I had never taken a trip just for myself. Last April I finally got the chance. I booked five days in Japan and told nobody at the office until the day I left.

The first two days were ordinary in the best way. I walked, I got lost, I ate alone. On the third morning I woke up early and went to a small temple outside the city. There was nobody there. That hour was the highlight of the whole trip, and I have never forgotten it.
I got homesick on day four. I called my sister and she laughed at me. Then she asked the right question: would you do it again? I said yes before she finished the sentence.

Ever since that trip I have kept a list on my phone. Some people call it a bucket list; I call it a promise. Kyoto was a once in a lifetime morning, and the whole thing was worthwhile — but I have learned that the next one does not have to wait five years.
